section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: How do we know any of what happened when farming began? No one alive today watched wild wheat slowly become farmed wheat. The answer is archaeologyar-kee-OL-uh-jeethe careful study of the things people leave behind: buildings, tools, seeds, bones, and trash., the careful study of the things people leave behind: buildings, tools, seeds, bones, and trash. Archaeologists do not simply dig for treasure. They perform an excavationek-skuh-VAY-shuna slow, careful dig, done layer by layer, that records exactly where and how deep every object was found., a slow, careful dig done layer by layer. They record exactly where every object was found, and how deep, because the depth of a layer usually tells you its age compared to the layers above and below it. When people build, abandon, and rebuild on the same spot for thousands of years, the site grows upward into a mound called a tellrhymes with "bell"a mound formed when people build, abandon, and rebuild on the same spot for thousands of years, so the site grows upward like a layered cake.. Travel across the Middle East today and you will see dozens of these grassy or dusty hills. Each one is a stack of ancient towns, waiting to be read like the pages of a book, with the oldest page on the bottom.
📚 JERICHO: WALLS BEFORE POTTERY

One of the greatest tells anywhere sits at Jericho, near the Jordan River in the region called the Levant. In the early 1950s, the British archaeologist **Kathleen Kenyon** dug deep into Jericho's mound. She found something startling: a massive stone tower, more than eight meters tall, attached to a thick stone wall. The wall and tower date to roughly 8000 BC. This makes Jericho one of the oldest walled settlements ever found, built before people had even invented pottery.

Why build a monument like this so early? This was before writing, before the wheel, before fired clay pots. Kenyon herself argued over the answer. A wall to keep out raiders is the obvious guess. But some archaeologists think the wall might have held back flash floods or mudslides instead. Others think the tower had some special role in Jericho's rituals, a role we do not fully grasp today. This is worth sitting with honestly. Sometimes the physical evidence is clear, but the human reason behind it is not. That gap, between what we can prove and what we can only guess, is part of what makes history a subject built on careful reasoning. It is not simple fact-finding.
🏙️ CITIES · JERICHO
Photo: CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Picture a walled settlement of simple mudbrick and stone houses clustered around a single massive stone tower built into the settlement's thick outer wall. No streets ran in straight lines. Paths wound between houses built close together, with fields of wheat and barley just outside the wall, watered by a nearby freshwater spring.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · KATHLEEN KENYON
Photo: courtesy UCL Institute of Archaeology, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

**Kathleen Kenyon** 🔊KATH-leen KEN-yunBritish archaeologist who led the excavation of Jericho. was a British archaeologist who led the major excavation of Jericho in the early 1950s. Her careful, layer-by-layer digging techniques helped set the standard for how archaeologists still excavate sites today. Her discovery of Jericho's ancient tower and wall reshaped what historians understood about how early humans first settled into permanent life.
📚 ÇATALHÖYÜK: A TOWN WITHOUT STREETS

About a thousand years later, several hundred kilometers north, a very new kind of Neolithic town grew up at Çatalhöyük, in what is now central Turkey. The British archaeologist **James Mellaart** began digging there in the 1960s. He found a town with no streets at all. Its mudbrick houses were built wall to wall, packed together like a honeycomb. Residents did not enter their homes through a front door. Instead, they climbed down a ladder through a hole in the roof, walking across the rooftops of the whole town to get from house to house.

Inside many homes, Mellaart's team found painted walls showing hunting scenes. They also found startling **bucrania**, the horned skulls of wild cattle, set into walls and platforms. Archaeologists still argue over exactly what these skulls meant to the people who placed them there, though most agree they held some ritual or family meaning.
🏙️ CITIES · ÇATALHÖYÜK
Photo: Zde, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Imagine a town with no streets or doors at ground level at all. Flat-roofed mudbrick houses packed together wall to wall, so closely that people walked across the rooftops to get anywhere, climbing down ladders through roof holes into rooms with wall paintings and the horned skulls of wild cattle.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · JAMES MELLAART
No verified public-domain or openly-licensed solo portrait of Mellaart could be confirmed for this page; a photo is omitted here rather than risking an uncleared image.

**James Mellaart** 🔊JAYMZ MEL-artBritish archaeologist who began digging at Çatalhöyük in 1961. was a British archaeologist who began digging at Çatalhöyük in 1961. His work turned up one of the best-kept Neolithic towns ever found, including its painted walls and cattle-skull shrines. Mellaart's finds remain central to how historians picture daily life in an early farming town.

section: WHAT A REPORT CAN AND CANNOT TELL YOU
text: 📚 WHAT A REPORT CAN AND CANNOT TELL YOU

section: WHAT A REPORT CAN AND CANNOT TELL YOU
text: Here is an important idea for how to read sources. Kenyon's and Mellaart's excavation reports are **primary sources**, but only about the dig itself. What Kenyon wrote is a firsthand, eyewitness account of what her team actually found in the ground at Jericho in the 1950s. That much is primary evidence, the direct word of someone who was there. But neither Kenyon nor Mellaart lived during the Neolithic period they were digging up. Their reports are **secondary evidence** about the Neolithic itself. They are careful, expert readings of physical clues, not eyewitness memories of Neolithic life. Ask yourself this question about any source you read: is this person a firsthand witness to the event I actually care about? Or is this person an expert explaining evidence about it long after the fact?

section: WHAT A REPORT CAN AND CANNOT TELL YOU
text: Jericho sits at roughly 31.9 degrees north latitude and 35.4 degrees east longitude, near the Jordan River valley. Çatalhöyük sits much farther north and slightly west, at roughly 37.7 degrees north latitude and 32.8 degrees east longitude, on the Anatolian plateau. Take a moment with a world map or atlas and plot both points. Notice how far apart they are, and yet how similar their basic story is. In two separate corners of the Fertile Crescent's wider neighborhood, small bands of people chose to settle down for good, within about a thousand years of each other, without ever meeting. That is not just luck, and it is not the work of two clever people acting alone. It is what happens when a deeper shift, the slow domestication of plants and animals, finally reaches a tipping point.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

Jericho's wall and Çatalhöyük's rooftop streets look nothing alike, but both mark the same turning point: people who had committed to staying in one place for good, building something meant to outlast a single lifetime. That commitment, sedentism, is the quiet foundation beneath every city, kingdom, or empire that follows.

📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
Can a people survive losing their king, their temple, and their homeland all at once?

The kingdoms of Israel and Judah deserve fuller attention. This lesson gives them fuller attention, first as a small kingdom caught between great powers, crushed and exiled by Nebuchadnezzar, and second as a set of religious beliefs, monotheism and covenant, genuinely different from the other religions of the ancient Near East. Against every expectation, Judah's identity survived exile with no king, no temple, and no homeland to anchor it.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: The kingdoms of Israel and Judah deserve fuller attention. This lesson gives them the fuller attention their history deserves. It looks at them two ways. First, as a small kingdom caught between great powers. Second, as a set of religious beliefs worth understanding on their own terms.
📚 A KINGDOM STANDING ALONE

By the seventh century BC, the northern kingdom of Israel no longer existed as its own state at all. Assyria had destroyed it in 722 BC. Assyria's kings also deported much of its people, a policy conquerors used to stop conquered peoples from planning future revolts. That left only the smaller southern kingdom, **Judah**, ruled from **Jerusalem**. For over a century, Judah worked hard just to survive between Egyptian and Mesopotamian power.

Judah's independence finally ended under Nebuchadnezzar II. According to a Babylonian chronicleKRON-ih-kula written record of events, usually listed year by year in plain, factual order., his forces captured Jerusalem in 597 BC. They carried off its king, a young ruler named Jehoiachin. Much of its elite population went with him to Babylon. Cuneiform ration tablets found in Babylon actually name Jehoiachin directly. These tablets list food handed out to royal prisoners there. This is a rare case where an outside, non-biblical record backs up a specific detail from this story. In other words, we do not have to take this story only on faith. A real object backs it up.

Nebuchadnezzar placed a new king, Zedekiah, on Judah's throne in Jehoiachin's place, expecting loyalty in return. A later Judean revolt tested Nebuchadnezzar's patience past its limit. His response was final and harsh. Zedekiah was captured. He was forced to watch his own sons killed. Then he was blinded, and carried off to Babylon himself. In 586 BC, Jerusalem itself was destroyed, along with its Temple, the central site of Israelite worship. A further wave of its people was deported to Babylon, beginning the period Jewish tradition remembers as the Babylonian exilebeing forced to leave your home country, often for a long time or forever, usually by a conquering power..
👥 PEOPLES · THE ISRAELITES AND JUDAHITES
Illustration: from the *Encyclopaedia Biblica*, 1903, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

The **Israelites**, and later the people of the southern kingdom of JudahJOO-duha small kingdom in the southern Levant, ruled from Jerusalem, conquered by Babylon., worshipped one god and lived under a covenant law they believed bound them together as a single people. This relief, depicting Near Eastern captives deported by a conquering empire, illustrates the kind of forced exile Judah's own people experienced under Babylon.

section: A BELIEF WORTH UNDERSTANDING ON ITS OWN TERMS
text: 📚 A BELIEF WORTH UNDERSTANDING ON ITS OWN TERMS

section: A BELIEF WORTH UNDERSTANDING ON ITS OWN TERMS
text: Israelite religion stands out against its neighbors. Sumerian, Egyptian, and Mesopotamian religion more broadly each recognized many gods with different jobs. These gods were often tied closely to nature, kingship, or a specific city. Israelite religion, as shown in its own surviving texts, worked differently. It centered on monotheismMON-oh-thee-iz-umbelief in and worship of only one god., devotion to a single god, and on a covenantKUV-uh-nunta binding, two-way agreement, often between a god and a people, with promised duties on both sides.. A covenant was a binding, mutual agreement, just between that god and the Israelite people. Under its terms, loyalty and obedience to a shared law were understood to carry real weight. Good or bad, that weight would show up in the community's own fortunes across history. In other words, Israel's own story was tied to how well its people kept their promise to their god.

section: A BELIEF WORTH UNDERSTANDING ON ITS OWN TERMS
text: Prophets living through this very crisis wrote and preached in exactly these terms. Jeremiah was still in Jerusalem as the city fell. He warned that the coming disaster was a direct result of the people breaking their own covenant. Ezekiel had already been sent to Babylon, years earlier. He wrote visions trying to make sense of that same disaster from exile itself. Reading their words is one clear way to see this covenant idea used in real time. Real people living through these very events used it. It was not some distant historian summing things up long after the fact. In other words, we are not just reading a summary written after the fact. We are reading words from people living through it.

🎯 TRY IT: TWO KINDS OF BELIEF Sort each feature by the religious system it describes. Many gods, each often tied to a particular city, natural force, or aspect of kingship. Mesopotamian and Egyptian p
section: A BELIEF WORTH UNDERSTANDING ON ITS OWN TERMS
A BELIEF WORTH UNDERSTANDING ON ITS OWN TERMS
text: This is a truly different kind of belief. It is not simply the same kind of belief as its neighbors, with the names changed. It deserves to be taken seriously as its own thing. It should not be flattened into some version of Mesopotamian or Egyptian religion. At the same time, this lesson does not claim to settle any question of religious truth, one way or another. Here is what can be said with confidence, as a matter of history rather than belief itself: Israelite writers often explained their kingdom's own defeats, including this one, as tied directly to this covenant. That framework is worth understanding honestly on its own terms. It should not get turned into some other civilization's own terms instead.
🏙️ CITIES · JERUSALEM
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Jerusalemjuh-ROO-suh-lemJudah's capital city, home to its Temple, destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar's forces in 586 BC., capital of the kingdom of Judah, was home to the Temple, the central site of Israelite worship. Nebuchadnezzar's forces destroyed both the city and the Temple in 586 BC, beginning the Babylonian exile. Modern excavations in the City of David, shown here, continue to uncover layers of the ancient city.

section: AN ENDING THAT WAS NOT, IN FACT, AN ENDING
text: 📚 AN ENDING THAT WAS NOT, IN FACT, AN ENDING

section: AN ENDING THAT WAS NOT, IN FACT, AN ENDING
text: Exile is a form of forced migration. It might reasonably have meant the end of Judah's people and beliefs for good. They could have simply melted into the wider Babylonian population, the way conquered peoples sometimes did vanish from the record entirely. That is not what happened here. Religious and cultural identity survived through decades of exile in Babylon itself. It stayed alive without a king, a temple, or even a homeland to anchor it. This is a truly rare outcome, worth noting rather than assumed. In other words, losing a homeland did not mean losing who they were.

section: AN ENDING THAT WAS NOT, IN FACT, AN ENDING
text: Its return, when it came, arrived from an unexpected direction. In 538 BC, a new conqueror had just taken Babylon itself. He issued a decree. That decree let Judean exiles return home and rebuild their Temple. This was a policy very different from the policies of Assyria or Babylon. That conqueror's name was **Cyrus**. In other words, the empire that conquered Babylon did not treat Judah's exiles the way Babylon had.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

Exile could easily have meant the end of Judah's people and beliefs. It did not. When return finally came, it arrived from an unexpected direction: a new conqueror named Cyrus, who held his empire together in a very different way.

There are some vocabulary words in this lesson worth reviewing.
colony🔊KOL-uh-neea settlement founded by people from another land, still linked back to its home city by trade and culture.
maritime commerce🔊MAIR-ih-time KOM-ursstrade carried across the sea by ships.
Tyrian purple🔊TEER-ee-una costly purple dye Phoenicians made from crushed sea snails.
alphabet🔊AL-fuh-beta writing system where each symbol stands for one sound, not a whole word or idea.

🗺️ MAIN MAP · PHOENICIA AND THE MEDITERRANEAN SEA Map: User:Rodrigo / User:Reedside, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. This map traces the Phoenician coast and its trade routes across the Mediterra
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
Can a people become the most important power in a region without ever building an empire?

When the Bronze Age Collapse tore through the Near East, most great powers on the map either fell or came out badly hurt. One place did not. A narrow strip of coastline in the Levant, home to a handful of small port cities, made it through mostly unharmed. Over the next few centuries, those cities did something remarkable. Without conquering anyone, they quietly became the busiest traders in the whole Mediterranean world. In other words, while bigger powers were still picking up the pieces, these small cities were already back in business.

text: **I will be able to** explain how being useful, rather than strong in arms, can help a civilization survive.
📚 CITIES, NOT AN EMPIRE

Phoeniciafuh-NEE-shuha narrow strip of coastline in the modern Levant, home to a string of independent trading cities. was never one single kingdom, the way Egypt or Assyria was. It was a group of independent city-states along the Levant coast. Each city had its own king, its own harbor, and its own fleet. They worked together when it helped them. They competed when it did not. This pattern should sound familiar. It is close to the pattern of Sumerian cities like Uruk: separate centers held together more by shared culture and trade than by any single crown. In other words, no one king ever ruled all of Phoenicia at once. Phoenicia's cities had little land and no great army. What they lacked in territory, they made up for in ships.

Phoenician sailors became the finest navigators and shipbuilders anywhere on the Mediterranean Sea. Using tall, prized stands of Lebanese cedar, they built strong ships that could cross open water other peoples avoided. Phoenician traders carried glassware and fine metalwork. Above all, they carried Tyrian purpleTEER-ee-una costly purple dye Phoenicians made from crushed sea snails., a costly dye pulled drop by drop from the crushed glands of a small sea snail. This dye cost so much that its color became a mark of royalty for centuries afterward, all the way into the Roman Empire. Phoenician traders needed tin to make bronze, but had none of their own. So they pushed steadily west, planting trading posts and coloniesKOL-uh-neea settlement founded by people from another land, still linked back to its home city by trade and culture. along the North African coast, in Sicily and Sardinia, and as far as the Strait of Gibraltar and the Iberian coast beyond it. This whole far-reaching system of ships, ports, and trade goods is what is meant by maritime commerceMAIR-ih-time KOM-ursstrade carried across the sea by ships..
🎯 TRY IT: PHOENICIA'S GOODS Match each description to the good it describes. A raw material essential for making bronze, which drove Phoenician traders to colonize as far west as Iberia. Tin Lebanese
👥 PEOPLES · THE PHOENICIANS
Photo: Emna Mizouni, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The **Phoenicians** were a Semitic-speaking people of the Levant coast, organized into independent trading city-states rather than one kingdom. This relief, carved on the sarcophagus of King Ahiram of Byblos, shows Phoenician dress and courtly life. Their ships, dye, and alphabet spread across the whole Mediterranean world.
📚 A DIFFERENT KIND OF GIFT

Phoenicia's most lasting gift to the wider world was not a good at all. It was a tool. Egyptian hieroglyphics and Mesopotamian cuneiform each needed scribes to master hundreds of different signs. The alphabetAL-fuh-beta writing system where each symbol stands for one sound, not a whole word or idea. the Phoenicians built and spread used only about twenty-two simple symbols. Each one stood for a single consonant sound. In other words, it was simply easier to learn. A trading network stretched across the whole Mediterranean was exactly the kind of place an easier writing system could spread fast. It moved port to port, carried by merchants, not just kept inside temple and palace walls. Within a few centuries, Greek traders picked up this same alphabet. They adapted it further, adding their own vowel signs. That adapted Greek alphabet is, eventually, the distant ancestor of the one used to write this very sentence. In other words, a system built for busy merchants counting cargo ended up shaping how nearly the whole Western world reads and writes today.
🏙️ CITIES · TYRE, SIDON, AND BYBLOS
Photo: RomanDeckert, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

**Tyre**, **Sidon**, and **Byblos** were Phoenicia's three leading port cities. Tyre, built partly on an island, was the wealthiest and later withstood a thirteen-year siege by Nebuchadnezzar II without being destroyed.
📚 VALUABLE ENOUGH TO SPARE

Phoenicia's story took a harder turn in the sixth century BC. Babylon's king Nebuchadnezzar II, builder of the Ishtar Gate and destroyer of Jerusalem, now turned toward the coast. Starting around 585 BC, Nebuchadnezzar laid siege to Tyrethe wealthiest of the Phoenician port cities, built partly on an island just off the coast. itself, the richest of the Phoenician cities. Tyre was built partly on an island and guarded by its own strong navy. The siege dragged on for roughly thirteen years, an amazing length of time by any ancient measure. Yet Tyre was never actually destroyed the way Jerusalem was. Surviving accounts say the siege ended in a deal. Tyre accepted Babylonian overlordship and likely paid tribute, but kept its own king, its own walls, and its own fleet mostly whole. In other words, Nebuchadnezzar's army camped outside Tyre's walls for thirteen full years and still could not force the city to surrender outright.

This is worth pausing on, using the same question raised by Assyria's terror and Babylon's grandeur: what actually holds a state together? Phoenicia's cities never built anything close to the war machine of Assyria. They never tried to hold land the way Egypt or Babylon did either. What kept Tyre standing through a thirteen-year siege was not strength of arms. It was being too valuable to destroy. Phoenicia controlled Mediterranean shipping, shipbuilding know-how, and a trade network no conquering power wanted to burn down along with the city. In other words, a city can sometimes protect itself just by being too useful to lose. A civilization can secure its own survival through being needed just as surely as through walls and armies, and sometimes more surely still. Compare this directly with Assyria's approach. Assyria ruled by fear and lost everything within a single generation once its army faltered. Phoenicia never had a strong army to begin with, and yet it outlasted Assyria anyway.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND
Phoenicia never built an army like Assyria's, yet it outlasted Assyria's entire empire by being too useful to destroy.

📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
What do two rival cities look like before either one knows the other exists?

Somewhere in the eighth century BC, by the old count ancient people themselves used, two cities were founded on opposite shores of the central Mediterranean. Neither city was much to look at yet. Neither founder had any idea the other city even existed. Neither knew what it would someday become. Centuries later, their own people would fight three long wars over which of them would survive at all.

text: **I will be able to** explain why neither city's founders could have known what Rome and Carthage would become.
📚 DIDO AND THE NEW CITY

Carthage was the greatest of the Phoenician colonies. It was planted on the North African coast, not far from modern Tunis. Its own name, in Phoenician, meant simply "New City." The oldest surviving version of its founding story comes from a later writer named Justin. In it, a Tyrian princess named DidoDY-doha Tyrian princess said to have fled Phoenicia and founded Carthage around 814 BC., sometimes called Elissa, fled her home city. Her own brother, King Pygmalion of Tyre, had killed her husband for his wealth. Dido sailed west with a band of loyal followers. She struck a shrewd, tricky deal with the local Berber ruler over how much land her new settlement could claim. Through that deal, she founded Carthage on the North African shore. Old tradition dates this founding to 814 BC.

Centuries later, the Roman poet Virgil told a very different version of Dido's story. His epic, the *Aeneid*, was written under the emperor Augustus. In Virgil's telling, Dido falls in love with the Trojan hero Aeneas, blown ashore at Carthage while fleeing the fall of Troy. She kills herself in despair when he sails on toward Italy to found the line that will one day become Rome. This version is fine writing, but it cannot be real history, and that should be said plainly. The Trojan War, whatever its real kernel, belongs to an age centuries before 814 BC. That is the very Bronze Age that had collapsed centuries before. Virgil knew this well. He was not making a mistake. He was writing centuries after Rome and Carthage had already fought their real wars. He used this anachronismuh-NAK-ruh-niz-uma detail placed in the wrong time period, out of its real historical order., a detail placed in the wrong time on purpose, to suggest that Rome's later hate for Carthage was somehow set into both cities' fates from the very start. It is a poet's point, not a historian's claim, and that gap matters.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · DIDO
Painting: J.M.W. Turner, 1815, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

DidoDY-doha Tyrian princess said to have fled Phoenicia and founded Carthage around 814 BC. (DY-doh), also called Elissa, is remembered as the Tyrian princess who fled Phoenicia after her brother murdered her husband, and founded Carthage on the North African coast around 814 BC. This 1815 painting by J.M.W. Turner imagines the rising city under construction.

section: ROMULUS, REMUS, AND A CITY BUILT ON A KILLING
text: 📚 ROMULUS, REMUS, AND A CITY BUILT ON A KILLING

section: ROMULUS, REMUS, AND A CITY BUILT ON A KILLING
text: Rome's own founding legend is kept most fully by the Roman historian Livy. According to Livy, twin brothers named RomulusROM-yoo-lustwin brother, with Remus, whose legend credits them with founding Rome in 753 BC. and RemusREE-mustwin brother, with Romulus, whose legend credits them with founding Rome in 753 BC. were born to Rhea Silvia. Her uncle **Amulius** had seized the throne of the nearby city of Alba Longa from her father, **Numitor**. Amulius forced Rhea Silvia into a role meant to leave her childless, so she could never bear a rival to his throne. Fearing the twins anyway as future rivals, Amulius ordered them drowned in the Tiber RiverTY-burthe river in central Italy on whose banks Rome was traditionally founded.. The basket carrying them instead washed ashore near the Palatine HillPAL-uh-tyneone of Rome's seven hills, where tradition says the she-wolf found and nursed Romulus and Remus.. There, tradition says, a she-wolf nursed the boys. A shepherd named Faustulus later found the twins and raised them as his own sons.

section: ROMULUS, REMUS, AND A CITY BUILT ON A KILLING
text: Notice how closely this echoes an older story from Mesopotamia. An infant is set adrift on a river. He is saved against every chance. He is meant for far more than his own humble rescuers could have guessed. That is almost exactly the shape of Sargon's basket story. This does not prove that one story copied the other. It shows instead that this kind of story, a low, uncertain start hiding a great future, appealed to ancient people again and again, in far-apart cultures with no contact at all.

🎯 TRY IT: ROME'S FOUNDING CAST Match each name to who they are in Livy's account. The rightful ruler of Alba Longa, overthrown by his own brother, later restored to his throne by his grandsons. Faustu
section: ROMULUS, REMUS, AND A CITY BUILT ON A KILLING
ROMULUS, REMUS, AND A CITY BUILT ON A KILLING
text: Grown to manhood, Romulus and Remus restored their grandfather Numitor to his throne. They then set out to found a city of their own, near where they had washed ashore. Rome itself rose in a part of Italy already shared with other peoples. Etruscan cities lay just to the north, and their customs shaped early Rome deeply. Greek trading colonies lay further south, in Sicily and along Italy's coast. The Greeks themselves called this whole southern cluster *Magna Graecia* MAG-nuh GREE-shuh"Greater Greece," the Greek trading colonies of southern Italy and Sicily., "Greater Greece." Livy's account of the twins does not end happily, though. The brothers argued bitterly over exactly where their new city's sacred boundary line, the **pomerium**, should run. Remus mocked his brother by leaping over the low wall Romulus had begun to mark out. In Livy's telling, Romulus killed his own twin brother on the spot for it. He said the same fate awaited anyone else who dared cross Rome's border uninvited. Tradition dates this founding, and this fratricideFRAT-rih-sydethe killing of one's own brother or sister., to 753 BC. Rome, in other words, begins its own story with a killing its own writers never tried to hide.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · ROMULUS AND REMUS
Sculpture: Capitoline Museums, Rome, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

RomulusROM-yoo-lustwin brother, with Remus, whose legend credits them with founding Rome in 753 BC. and RemusREE-mustwin brother, with Romulus, whose legend credits them with founding Rome in 753 BC. were twin brothers whose legend credits them with founding Rome in 753 BC. Left to drown as infants and saved by a she-wolf, Romulus went on to kill his own brother in a quarrel over the new city's boundary. This bronze sculpture, the Capitoline Wolf, is one of Rome's most famous images of the story.
🏙️ CITIES · CARTHAGE AND ROME
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

**Carthage**, on the North African coast, and **Rome**, on the Tiber River in central Italy, were both founded as small, precarious settlements in the eighth century BC. Neither city's founders could have guessed the two would one day fight for control of the whole Mediterranean.
📚 CLOSING

Set side by side, these two founding stories share a striking pattern: exile, hardship, and a small, uncertain settlement built by people fleeing worse trouble elsewhere. Neither Dido's followers nor Romulus's shepherds could have imagined that their two cities would someday stand as the Mediterranean's two greatest rival powers. That struggle would not begin in earnest for another five and a half centuries. In other words, the story leaves both cities here, at their small and shaky start, long before either one becomes a name the whole Mediterranean world would fear or admire. What belongs here is the beginning: two foundling cities, born the same rough century, each certain only of its own small patch of shore.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

Two foundling cities, born the same rough century, each certain only of its own small patch of shore. Neither Dido's followers nor Romulus's shepherds could have imagined the two would someday fight for the whole Mediterranean.

text: 📖 GLOSSARY OF SUBJECT VOCABULARY
There are some vocabulary words in this lesson worth reviewing.
contingency🔊kun-TIN-jen-seethe idea that history could easily have turned out differently, because it depended on small, uncertain events, not one fixed path.
dynasty🔊DY-nuh-steea line of rulers from the same family, passing power down from parent to child.
empire🔊EM-pyrea single political power that rules over many different peoples, cities, and languages at once.

🗺️ MAIN MAP · THE AKKADIAN EMPIRE Map: Zunkir, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. This map shows Sargon's growing reach, from Kish and Uruk in southern Mesopotamia, north and west through Akkad 🔊 AH
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
Could one basket on a river really stand at the root of the first empire?

Earlier civilizations such as Jericho, Çatalhöyük, and Uruk were each a single city or a small region. Then a man named Sargon built something the world had never seen: an empire ruling many cities and peoples at once. The story his own scribes told about his birth is strange, humble, and possibly half legend, and it is the perfect place to ask how much of history really turns on small, uncertain events instead of one fixed path.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: Earlier civilizations such as Jericho, Çatalhöyük, and Uruk were each a single city or a single small region. Then that changed. Around 2334 BC, a man named Sargon🔊SAR-gonfounder of the Akkadian Empire, the first empire in recorded history, ruling from roughly 2334 to 2279 BC. built something the world had never seen before: an empireEM-pyrea single political power that rules over many different peoples, cities, and languages at once.. An empire is a single political power that rules over many separate cities and peoples at once. Sargon's empire stretched across all of Mesopotamia and beyond. To understand how strange and unlikely this feat was, you have to start with the story Sargon himself, or scribes writing in his name years later, told about his own birth.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

**Sargon** 🔊SAR-gonfounder of the Akkadian Empire, the first empire in recorded history, ruling from roughly 2334 to 2279 BC. is this lesson's central figure, founder of the world's first known empire.
📚 AN IMPROBABLE BEGINNING

According to the Sargon Birth Legend, Sargon was born to a priestess who could not openly raise him. She placed her infant son in a basket sealed with tar and set him adrift on the Euphrates River. The basket floated downstream until a man named Akki, a drawer of water, found it. Akki rescued the child and raised him as his own son, later training him as a gardener. From this humble, obscure beginning, the story says, the goddess Ishtar came to favor young Sargon. He rose to become cupbearer, a position of real trust and access, to the king of the city of Kish. From cupbearer, Sargon eventually seized power for himself. He then began the conquests that built the Akkadian Empire and founded his own royal dynastyDY-nuh-steea line of rulers from the same family, passing power down from parent to child..

Whether every detail of this story happened exactly as told is hard to check for sure. No other written record from Sargon's own lifetime lives on to check the story against. Here is what matters for how you think about history: the entire empire that follows rests on a chain of events that did not have to happen. What if the basket had sunk? What if Akki had not been drawing water at that exact bend of the river that day? What if Sargon had never caught the king's eye? If any one of these small things had gone differently, none of the rest of this lesson would exist to tell. This is what historians mean by contingencykun-TIN-jen-seethe idea that history could easily have turned out differently, because it depended on small, uncertain events, not one fixed path.: the real past was not marching toward Sargon's empire like some fixed endpoint it had to reach. A single unlikely childhood, real or made up, stands at the root of the first empire in recorded history.
📚 FROM CUPBEARER TO CONQUEROR

Once in power, Sargon moved with real speed. He conquered the Sumerian city-states one by one, including Uruk. He defeated Uruk's king, Lugalzagesi, and brought the whole of southern Mesopotamia under one rule for the first time. He then pushed his conquests northward and westward, as far as the Mediterranean coast, and into parts of Anatolia and Elam. Sargon founded a new capital city, Akkad. Its exact spot has never been found again by archaeologists, a small but telling reminder: even a capital city ruling an empire can vanish from the map while still living on in written memory.

section: WHY "EMPIRE" IS A NEW KIND OF WORD
text: 📚 WHY "EMPIRE" IS A NEW KIND OF WORD

section: WHY "EMPIRE" IS A NEW KIND OF WORD
text: It is worth pausing on why historians save the word empire for what Sargon built, rather than just calling it a large kingdom. A kingdom mostly rules one people, in one place, under one set of customs. An empire rules many different peoples, cities, and languages at once. These peoples did not always choose to be ruled together, and often kept their own local customs, gods, and leaders, even while bowing to one distant ruler. Sargon had no telephones, no fast roads, and no trained government passed down from anyone before him, since no one had ever built one this large.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · SARGON OF AKKAD
Photo: Hans Ollermann, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

**Sargon** rose from a humble, disputed birth to found the world's first known empire, ruling Mesopotamia and beyond from his capital at Akkad around 2334 to 2279 BC. His conquests united dozens of independent Sumerian city-states under a single ruler for the first time in recorded history, setting a pattern that later empires across the ancient world would imitate.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

Sargon's empire did not grow out of a plan anyone could have predicted from a basket on a river. It grew because a string of small, uncertain events broke his way, and because he then moved fast once in power. Ruling that many cities and peoples at once, though, is a very different problem from winning them.

There are some vocabulary words in this lesson worth reviewing.
code of law🔊a single, written collection of laws meant to apply the same way across an entire kingdom, rather than being decided case by case.
stele🔊STEE-leea tall, upright stone slab, often carved with writing or images, set up in a public place.
🗺️ MAIN MAP · BABYLON AND THE AMORITE MIGRATIONS Map: MapMaster, CC BY-SA, via Wikimedia Commons. This map shows the western desert and the Levant, where the Amorites migrated from, and marks Babylon
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
How does a minor town on the Euphrates become the capital of an age?

The Akkadian Empire ended in ruins, leaving behind a power vacuum. Migrating Amorite herders slowly took over Mesopotamia's cities, one of them a small, unremarkable town called Babylon. Nothing about Babylon marked it for greatness until a king named Hammurabi finished a long, cautious reign with a fast burst of conquest, and then left behind something that would outlast his empire itself: a written code of law.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: The Akkadian Empire's collapse left a power vacuum across Mesopotamia. No single city held the kind of power Sargon or Naram-Sin once held. Into this shaken land, over the next centuries, came waves of a people the Mesopotamians called the **Amorites** (AM-uh-ryts). The Amorites were herders who moved from place to place and spoke a Semitic language. They came in from the western desert and the Levant, starting around 2000 to 1900 BC. Amorite chiefs and their followers slowly settled among the Mesopotamian cities already there, sometimes simply taking the cities over, but keeping the old language, writing system, and faith already in place.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: Some Amorite groups still lived in tents even after their own kings sat on Mesopotamian thrones. Letters found in the city of Mari describe this mixed way of life in real detail: part herder, part city ruler, all at once. Within just a few generations, Amorite kings wrote in cuneiform, prayed to Mesopotamian gods, and ruled from Mesopotamian palaces like anyone born there.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

**Hammurabi** 🔊hah-moo-RAH-beethe Amorite king of Babylon, ruling roughly 1792 to 1750 BC, best known today for his written code of law., the Amorite king of Babylon, ruling roughly 1792 to 1750 BC, best known today for his written code of law.
📚 A MINOR CITY RISES

Among the many small city-states an Amorite family came to rule was Babylon, a fairly small town on the Euphrates. At the start of the second millennium BC, Babylon had no special claim to greatness. That changed with the reign of Hammurabi, who took Babylon's throne around 1792 BC. For much of his reign, Hammurabi ruled a modest kingdom, careful and mostly on guard, forming and breaking deals with bigger neighbors as needed. Only late in his reign did this pattern change. In a fast series of wars during his final decade of rule, Hammurabi finally joined southern and much of central Mesopotamia under Babylon's rule, beating rival cities one after another, including Larsa, Mari, and Eshnunna, each of which had once been at least as strong as Babylon itself.

This timing matters. It would be easy to picture Hammurabi as a conqueror from the very start of his reign. The actual pattern was not that simple. Contingencythe idea that history could easily have turned out differently, because it depended on small, uncertain events, not one fixed path. shows up here too, just as it did with Sargon. If Hammurabi had died at fifty instead of ruling into his final years of war, Babylon might have stayed a middling kingdom, known today, if at all, as just one Amorite city-state among many.
📚 MORE THAN A CONQUEROR

Hammurabi's military wins are not what makes his reign matter most to history. He is best known today for something else instead: a written code of lawa single, written collection of laws meant to apply the same way across an entire kingdom, rather than being decided case by case.. This code was carved onto a huge stone steleSTEE-leea tall, upright stone slab, often carved with writing or images, set up in a public place. and set up in public. Hammurabi's Code survives largely whole today, nearly four thousand years later, covering nearly every part of daily life: family, land, work, farming, and trade. It also clearly frames Hammurabi's rule around one central promise: justice for his subjects.

section: HELPFUL TO KNOW A NOTE ON CHRONOLOGY
text: 💡 HELPFUL TO KNOW · A NOTE ON CHRONOLOGY

section: HELPFUL TO KNOW A NOTE ON CHRONOLOGY
text: Historians place Hammurabi's reign at roughly 1792 to 1750 BC using the "Middle Chronology," one of several rival dating systems scholars use for the ancient Near East. A Babylonian record of the planet Venus, kept by ancient sky-watchers, is one key piece of evidence scholars compare against modern star charts to test rival systems. The Middle Chronology is used throughout, but other textbooks may use a different one.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · HAMMURABI
Photo: Mbzt, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

**Hammurabi** ruled Babylon from about 1792 to 1750 BC. He spent most of his reign as a careful, guarded king, only finishing his conquest of Mesopotamia in his final years of rule. He is known today mainly for his code of law, one of the most complete and best-kept law collections to survive from the ancient world.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

Babylon's rise, like Sargon's before it, did not have to happen. A late-life burst of conquest turned one Amorite king's cautious kingdom into the namesake of an entire age. But Hammurabi's real claim on history is the written code that followed the wars, and whether it delivered on its own promise of justice is a question worth testing.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: Assyria's empire was built through Ashurnasirpal II's terror and Shalmaneser III's steady growth. It reached its widest borders, and its greatest work of the mind, under one final king. His name was **Ashurbanipal**, and he ruled from roughly 668 to 627 BC. Under him, Assyria stretched from the Persian Gulf to the Nile. For a brief time, Assyria even ruled Egypt itself, after the sack of Thebes. But Ashurbanipal's most lasting achievement was not a conquest at all.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

**Ashurbanipal** 🔊ah-shur-BAH-nih-palking of Assyria from about 668 to 627 BC, whose library at Nineveh preserved thousands of Mesopotamian texts., king of Assyria from about 668 to 627 BC, whose library at Nineveh preserved thousands of Mesopotamian texts.

section: A KING WHO LEARNED TO READ
text: 📚 A KING WHO LEARNED TO READ

section: A KING WHO LEARNED TO READ
text: Assyrian kings were warriors first. Ashurbanipalah-shur-BAH-nih-palking of Assyria from about 668 to 627 BC, whose library at Nineveh preserved thousands of Mesopotamian texts. was no exception. He boasted in his own writings of hunting lions and leading campaigns. This was the same kind of proud royal language common in ancient royal inscriptions. Stone reliefs from his palace are among the finest carvings to survive from ancient Assyria. They show him hunting lions released from cages in a royal park. He spears and shoots them at close range, in front of a watching crowd. Scholars today often call these carvings the Lion Hunt reliefs. They were meant to show the king as Assyria's protector, brave enough to face its fiercest predator with his own hands.

section: A KING WHO LEARNED TO READ
text: In other words, Ashurbanipal wanted to be remembered two ways at once. He wanted to be seen as a fighter strong enough to face wild lions. He also wanted to be seen as a scholar wise enough to read the old gods' own words. But he also claims something highly unusual for a Mesopotamian king. He says he himself was taught to read and write cuneiform as a young prince. That was a skill normally left only to trained scribes. In his own words, he describes learning "the wisdom of Nabu." Nabu was the Mesopotamian god of writing and knowledge. He studied hard scholarly tablets in both Akkadian and the much older Sumerian language. By his own time, Sumerian had not been spoken aloud for well over a thousand years. Yet scribes still preserved it. They studied it and copied it, the way students today might treat a truly ancient classical language. In other words, Ashurbanipal studied a language that was, to him, already ancient history. This is much like a student today studying a language no one speaks anymore. The goal, then and now, is to unlock what it can still teach.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · ASHURBANIPAL
Photo: British Museum, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Ashurbanipalah-shur-BAH-nih-palking of Assyria from about 668 to 627 BC, whose library at Nineveh preserved thousands of Mesopotamian texts. ruled Assyria from about 668 to 627 BC. Unlike most Mesopotamian kings, he could personally read and write cuneiform, and he used his empire's resources to build the ancient world's largest known library at Nineveh.
📚 THE LIBRARY AT NINEVEH

Ashurbanipal used his position, and his empire's resources, to gather an enormous royal librarya planned collection of written tablets or scrolls, gathered and kept in one place for study and safekeeping. at his capital, NinevehNIN-uh-vuhAshurbanipal's royal capital, on the Tigris River, home to his great library.. He sent agents throughout Assyria, and above all into Babylonia, to collect, copy, and bring back tabletsa flat piece of clay, used across Mesopotamia for writing in cuneiform, often dried or baked hard afterward.. These tablets covered every subject: medicine, astronomy, omens, grammar, royal history, and story-poems. Modern archaeologists have found many thousands of tablets from this library. Among them is a nearly whole copy of the **Epic of Gilgamesh**, the same hero tale that began in Sumerian Uruk. It survives here in its fullest ancient form because Ashurbanipal's scribes thought it worth copying and keeping. Without this library, much of what scholars today know about Sumerian and Babylonian writing might simply be lost. In other words, one king's own curiosity ended up saving stories and knowledge that might otherwise have vanished forever.

Ashurbanipal's tablets often end with a **colophon**, a short scribal note naming the tablet's owner. Some colophons even warn future readers against removing or damaging the tablet, calling down the gods' anger on anyone who might steal from the collection. It is a small, very human detail. Here is a king proud enough of his library to threaten curses in its defense.

The library sat buried and forgotten for over two thousand years. British archaeologists, Austen Henry Layard and later Hormuzd Rassam, dug into Nineveh's ruins in the 1850s. They uncovered room after room packed with broken clay tablets, tens of thousands of pieces in all. Museum staff and scholars have spent well over a century sorting, matching, and translating these pieces. New pieces are still being matched and joined together even today. In other words, a library one king built was lost for over two thousand years. It was found again, and pieced back together, by people from a country Ashurbanipal never even knew existed.
🏙️ CITIES · NINEVEH
Illustration: Austen Henry Layard, *The Monuments of Nineveh*, 1853, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

NinevehNIN-uh-vuhAshurbanipal's royal capital, on the Tigris River, home to his great library., on the Tigris River, was Ashurbanipal's royal capital and home to his great library. It would be destroyed within a generation of his death.
⚠️ A WARNING BENEATH THE GLORY

Ashurbanipal's reign was not only lions and learning. Ashurbanipal's father had placed his own older brother, Shamash-shum-ukin, on the throne of Babylon as a separate, junior king. For several years, the two brothers fought a brutal civil war against each other. That war ended with Babylon besieged and Ashurbanipal's brother dead. It is worth naming plainly, since it hints at exactly the kind of danger that would later bring the empire down. Even at Assyria's proudest height, a fight within the royal family itself could shake the whole empire to its foundations. In other words, it was Ashurbanipal's own family, not some foreign enemy, that came closest to tearing his empire apart. This happened while he still sat on his own throne.
📚 AN IRONY WORTH SITTING WITH

Nineveh's palace, library included, would be destroyed by fire within a generation of Ashurbanipal's death. Fire almost always destroys writing. But clay tablets are different. They do not act like papyrus or parchment. The very fire that destroyed Ashurbanipal's palace baked his unbaked clay tablets hard. In effect, it fired them like pottery. This accident helped preserve thousands of tablets, shattered but largely whole, for archaeologists to recover and piece back together more than two thousand years later. By pure accident, a disaster that ended a king's dynasty also protected some of his greatest work. History rarely hands out its ironies this cleanly, but this one is real.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND
Even at Assyria's proudest height, a civil war within Ashurbanipal's own family nearly tore the empire apart from within, not from any foreign enemy.

text: Assyria grew strong enough to sack Thebes, deep inside Egyptian land, in 663 BC. This lesson goes back roughly two centuries earlier. It goes back to the king who did more than perhaps any other single ruler to build **Assyria** into a fearsome power. That power is what made a feat like the sack of Thebes possible. The king's name was **Ashurnasirpal II**. He ruled from roughly 883 to 859 BC.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

**Ashurnasirpal II** 🔊ah-shur-NAH-sir-palking of Assyria from about 883 to 859 BC, who built up Assyria's army and used public terror as a tool of state., king of Assyria from about 883 to 859 BC, who built up Assyria's army and used public terror as a tool of state.

section: A VACUUM WAITING TO BE FILLED
text: 📚 A VACUUM WAITING TO BE FILLED

section: A VACUUM WAITING TO BE FILLED
text: After the Bronze Age Collapse, Mesopotamia went more than two centuries without any one power strong enough to rule it all. Small, rival kingdoms fought for the upper hand across the region's north. None of them stayed strong enough to hold real control for long. Assyria itself had existed for a very long time, since well before Hammurabi's Babylon. But for most of that time, it was just one regional power among several others. It often paid tribute to whichever neighbor was strongest that year.

section: A VACUUM WAITING TO BE FILLED
text: Ashurnasirpal IIah-shur-NAH-sir-palking of Assyria from about 883 to 859 BC, who built up Assyria's army and used public terror as a tool of state. changed that. He rebuilt Assyria's army from the ground up. He moved his capital from the old religious city of Assur to a rebuilt city called Nimrudnim-ROODan ancient city on the Tigris that Ashurnasirpal II rebuilt as his royal capital., some fifty miles up the Tigris River. There, he raised a grand new palace. Huge stone statues guarded its gates: winged, human-headed bulls called lamassu. Each one was meant to frighten away evil and impress every visitor who passed beneath it. Ashurnasirpal began a string of conquests. His successors later grew these conquests into what historians call the **Neo-Assyrian Empire**. In time, this became the largest empire the Near East had yet seen. In other words, one determined king turned a middle-sized kingdom into the strongest power anyone in the region had ever seen.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · ASHURNASIRPAL II
Photo: Julesvernex2, British Museum, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Ashurnasirpal IIah-shur-NAH-sir-palking of Assyria from about 883 to 859 BC, who built up Assyria's army and used public terror as a tool of state. ruled Assyria from about 883 to 859 BC. He rebuilt Assyria's army, moved its capital to Nimrud, and used publicized, calculated violence as a deliberate tool of imperial control.
📚 TERROR BY DESIGN

Ashurnasirpal II left his own royal record. It records his campaigns in language that is, quite on purpose, meant to frighten. He describes skinning rebellious officials alive and hanging their skins on city walls. He describes setting captives on tall stakes outside a rebel city's gates. He describes building towers made from the skulls of defeated enemies, left standing at a city's edge as a lasting warning to travelers. He had all of these acts carved and openly recorded on palace walls and stone monuments. He did not hide them away out of shame.

This is worth pausing on directly, rather than looking past it. Ashurnasirpal was not simply cruel in some small, personal way. He used public, planned violence as a tool to rule his empire. It was a warning sent out to every city that might think about rebelling. Submit, pay tribute, and live. Or resist, and this is what will happen to you. His own annals name dozens of towns along the upper Tigris and Euphrates. Each one faced this same choice, one after another, as his armies pushed outward year after year. In other words, Ashurnasirpal was not hiding his cruelty at all. He wanted every city to hear about it, long before his army ever showed up at their gates.
👥 PEOPLES · THE ASSYRIANS
Photo: Northwest Palace of Nimrud, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

The **Assyrians** built their homeland along the upper Tigris River, in what is now northern Iraq. Under kings like Ashurnasirpal II, they built the ancient Near East's first true standing army and, in time, its largest empire yet. Stone reliefs like this one show Assyrian soldiers in their armor and helmets, with long curled beards, attacking a walled town.
📚 A QUESTION WORTH ASKING HONESTLY

A recurring question is whether a people's laws, customs, and habits help explain their success or failure at first-order political problems. Those problems include keeping internal peace, defending against outside threats, and binding a community together. Ashurnasirpal's terror clearly served the first two goals, at least for a time. Cities that had seen what happened to a rebellious neighbor thought twice before rising up themselves. Assyria's borders grew quickly and held firm for the rest of his reign.

But the third goal is harder to judge. Could terror bind a large, many-peopled empire into something like a shared political community? This lesson will not answer that fully yet. Fear can win a battle. Fear can even hold a province for a while. But can fear alone hold an empire together across generations, long after the king who inspired it is gone? Assyria's later history answers that question directly, when this same Assyrian empire, at the very height of its power, falls apart far faster than anyone watching it at its peak might have guessed. In other words, winning wars is not the same thing as building lasting loyalty. This lesson leaves that second, harder problem open on purpose.

section: TECHNOLOGY SPOTLIGHT ASSYRIA'S PROFESSIONAL STANDING ARMY
text: Assyria's year-round army, backed by iron weapons, siege engines, and cavalry, was a genuinely new kind of military institution in the ancient Near East, distinct from the seasonal levies of Sumer, Akkad, or Egypt. It let Assyria's kings campaign nearly every year without waiting for harvests to end, and it is the single biggest reason Assyria's empire grew as large, and as fast, as it did.
📚 BUILDING THE MACHINE

Ashurnasirpal's terror was backed by a truly new kind of army. Earlier armies, in Sumer, Akkad, or even New Kingdom Egypt, leaned heavily on seasonal levies. Farmers and townsmen were called up for one campaign, then sent home again once the fighting ended. Assyria built something different instead: a professional standing armya year-round, trained military force, kept ready at all times, rather than farmers and townsmen called up only for a single campaign.. Its soldiers were kept ready and paid all year round, rather than sent back to their fields. Its troops carried iron weapons rather than bronze, a real edge in strength over rivals still equipped the older way.

Special building crews built siege enginesa large machine, such as a battering ram or a tall movable tower, built to break through a city's walls.: battering rams and tall movable towers. These could break through even strong, thick city walls. Earlier armies could often only starve such a city into surrender, through a long blockade. Skilled cavalryKAV-uhl-reesoldiers who fight while mounted on horseback. units gave Assyria's kings something new too: soldiers fighting from horseback, rather than on foot or from chariots alone. This gave Assyria a fast-moving strike force that earlier Near Eastern armies had rarely fielded at this scale. Assyrian kings after Ashurnasirpal kept building and expanding this standing, professional machine for nearly two centuries. It is what let Assyria's later rulers reach as far as Egypt itself, sacking Thebes in 663 BC. In other words, Assyria did not just get lucky, over and over, in battle after battle. It built a genuinely new kind of army, one made to fight all year, every year, without stopping for the harvest.
🏙️ CITIES · NIMRUD
Photo: British Museum, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

Nimrudnim-ROODan ancient city on the Tigris that Ashurnasirpal II rebuilt as his royal capital., on the Tigris River, became Ashurnasirpal II's rebuilt royal capital. Its palace gates were guarded by huge stone lamassu, winged bulls with human heads, meant to frighten away evil and impress every visitor.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

Ashurnasirpal's terror and his new standing army together won Assyria fast, wide borders. Whether fear alone can hold an empire together across generations is a harder question this lesson leaves open on purpose.

📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
How do you invent writing, and why would a king list mix real history with legend?

Uruk's temple officials faced a real problem: too much grain, wool, and livestock to track by memory alone. This lesson follows that problem all the way to cuneiform, one of the most important inventions in human history, and then to the strange document that invention eventually made possible: the Sumerian King List, a record that mixes real kings with flood legends and impossibly long reigns.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: Uruk's temple officials faced a real problem. How do you keep track of a temple's grain, wool, and livestock once the numbers grow too large to hold in memory? Sumer's answer, grown slowly over centuries, became one of the biggest inventions in human history.
⚙️ TECHNOLOGY SPOTLIGHT · CUNEIFORM WRITING
Photo: LACMA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Long before anyone in Mesopotamia wrote a full sentence, temple officials used small clay tokens shaped like cones, spheres, and disks, each standing for an amount of grain, oil, or animals. By around 3300 BC, officials began pressing these tokens into wet clay, then drawing the token's shape directly into the clay with a reed stylus. Over centuries, these pictures grew simpler and could also stand for sounds, not just objects, becoming true writing. The wedge-shaped marks left by a reed stylus give this script its name: cuneiformkyoo-NEE-uh-forman early writing system made of wedge-shaped marks pressed into wet clay with a reed stylus., from the Latin word for "wedge-shaped." A person trained to read and write cuneiform, called a scribeSKRYBa person specially trained to read and write, one of the most respected jobs in Mesopotamian society., became one of the most valued and respected jobs in Mesopotamian society. Cuneiform was written in dozens of different tongues for roughly three thousand years, longer than any other writing system in world history has lasted.
📚 KINGSHIP DESCENDED FROM HEAVEN

Once cuneiform grew into a flexible tool, Sumerian scribes began writing down their own past. One of the most amazing records to survive is the **Sumerian King List**, a long record of cities and kings. In the scribes' own telling, this list stretches back before a great flood swept over the land. According to the list, "kingship descended from heaven" and was first held by the city of Eridu. From there, kingship passed from city to city among a handful of legendary rulers, reigning for tens of thousands of years each, before the flood came and swept everything away. After the flood, kingship "descended from heaven" a second time, passing to the city of Kish. From Kish onward, the reigns recorded shrink down to lengths a real human king could actually rule for.

What should a careful reader make of this? The King List mixes real historical memory, real cities in something close to a real order of political power, with clear legendLEJ-enda traditional story about the past that may contain some real memory, but is not treated as a strictly factual record.: reigns of impossible length, and a single giant flood that ends an entire age of the world. Sorting out these two threads with honesty, without tossing out either one, is one of the core skills of historical thinking.

Gilgamesh himself, the king credited with building Uruk's wall, is a perfect case of this mixing. He shows up on the King List as a real, historical ruler of Uruk's dynasty. Yet he is also the hero of the *Epic of Gilgamesh*, an epicEP-ika long poem about the adventures of a great hero, often mixing real memory with legend. poem built up over centuries. That poem gives him journeys, fights with monsters, and a quest for life without end that no historian treats as plain fact. A single figure can be both a real king remembered in an official record, and a legendary hero remembered in poetry, at the very same time.

The Epic of Gilgamesh includes its own flood story, told by a survivor named Utnapishtim. The Sumerian King List itself includes its own account of the flood and kingship's return afterward. Ask yourself which parts feel like memory, and which feel like legend, and why that distinction matters.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

Cuneiform turned a bookkeeping problem into the first written language in world history, and once scribes could write down anything, they wrote down their own past, memory and legend together. Sorting the two apart honestly, without throwing away either one, is exactly the skill good historians practice.

text: Hammurabi had a stele, a tall stone monument, carved with 282 laws and set up in a temple where his subjects could see it, or have it read to them. This lesson gives you the tools to evaluate what you will read there.

section: JUDGING A REGIME BY WHAT IT SOLVES
text: 📚 JUDGING A REGIME BY WHAT IT SOLVES

section: JUDGING A REGIME BY WHAT IT SOLVES
text: One good way historians judge an ancient government is to ask a very real question. Does it solve the basic problems every group of people faces? Does it set up stable offices whose power people actually trust? Does it apply common laws in a steady, fair way, rather than leaving justice to the whims of whoever happens to hold power?

section: JUDGING A REGIME BY WHAT IT SOLVES
text: Judged by these standards, Hammurabi's Code is a real win. It covers a huge range of daily life: contracts, wages, marriage, inheritance, and the duties of doctors, builders, and boat-builders. A trader, a farmer, or a family with a complaint had, at least in theory, a public, written rule to point to, rather than trusting only the private word of whichever local strongman happened to be in charge.

section: "AN EYE FOR AN EYE": PROPORTIONAL JUSTICE
text: 📚 "AN EYE FOR AN EYE": PROPORTIONAL JUSTICE

section: "AN EYE FOR AN EYE": PROPORTIONAL JUSTICE
text: The Code's most famous rule is eye-for-an-eye justice (*lex talionis*), Latin for "law of getting even." Under this rule, the punishment should match the harm done: an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a broken bone for a broken bone. Feuds and revenge killings, before written law, could spin far out past the size of the first wrong. Against that backdrop, lex talionis is a real limit on revenge. The law caps what a wronged side is allowed to take back, rather than leaving revenge open-ended.
📚 A REAL, BUT LIMITED, JUSTICE

At the same time, a close read of the Code shows something important: its justice was not the same for everyone. Babylonian society was split into set classes. The free citizen (*amelu*) held high or full legal rank. The commoner (*mushkenum*) was a free but lower class, with fewer legal shields, usually less than what an amelu paid or got. Slaves held the legal status of property under the law, not full legal rights as a person.

The same wound, an eye put out, a bone broken, carried a different fine, based on the class of both the victim and the one at fault. Hammurabi's Code gave real, steady, publicly known justice. At the very same time, it built unequal treatment right into its own bones. Both things are true at once, and a fair look at the Code has to hold both.
⚙️ TECHNOLOGY SPOTLIGHT · BABYLONIAN MATHEMATICS
Photo: Columbia University, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Babylonian math grew right out of the same money-keeping needs that gave us cuneiform writing. Babylonian scribes used a sexagesimal system, based on 60 rather than 10, which made it easy to split numbers into thirds, quarters, fifths, and sixths without messy fractions, part of why the number 60 still shows up in how we measure time and angles today. The clay tablet Plimpton 322, listing what math experts now call Pythagorean triples, shows scribes using a form of the Pythagorean theorem more than a thousand years before Pythagoras lived in Greece. This math grew out of the same scribe schools that trained the men who wrote laws like Hammurabi's Code.

section: TECHNOLOGY SPOTLIGHT SOCIAL CLASS UNDER THE CODE
text: ⚙️ TECHNOLOGY SPOTLIGHT · SOCIAL CLASS UNDER THE CODE

section: TECHNOLOGY SPOTLIGHT SOCIAL CLASS UNDER THE CODE
text: Hammurabi's Code named three broad classes of person, setting different fines and pay depending on which class was in a given case. The amelu held full legal rank: the top shields, and often the top fines for wronging one. The mushkenum, a free but lower class, got real legal shields, but at a lower level, with less pay owed for harm against them. Enslaved people held the least legal rank of all, treated under the law more like goods than like full legal persons, though the Code still set some small shields around their care. This layered system shows something key about Babylonian justice: it was real and steady, but it was never equal.
📚 KINGSHIP JUSTIFIED BY JUSTICE

Finally, notice how Hammurabi frames his own right to rule. He does not just claim power by force of arms. In the Code's prologue, Hammurabi presents himself as chosen by the gods, sent to "cause justice to prevail in the land," and to protect the weak from the strong. A king who bases his rule on justice, rather than on raw force alone, sets a real standard his own subjects, and history after them, can measure him against.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · HAMMURABI
Photo: Mbzt, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
**Hammurabi** is known less for his wars than for the code of law he left behind: a written promise that even a king's power should serve justice, not replace it.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

Hammurabi's Code was a genuine solution to a real political problem: steady, public, written law instead of a strongman's whim. It was also, at the very same time, a law that never treated all its subjects equally. Hold both facts together, rather than picking whichever one is easier to believe.

section: Why do empires fall apart, and who or what is really to blame?
text: Conquering dozens of independent Sumerian city-states, as Sargon did, is one problem. Governing them afterward, so they stay conquered, is a much harder one. This lesson looks at how the Akkadian Empire tried to solve that problem under Sargon's grandson, Naram-Sin, and then turns to a still-debated question: why, roughly a century and a half after Sargon's rise, did the empire collapse? An ancient poem blames one king's pride. Modern evidence points to drought and invasion. Both threads are worth taking seriously at once.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: Conquering dozens of independent Sumerian city-states, as Sargon did, is one problem. Governing them afterward, so they stay conquered, is a much harder one. This lesson looks at how the Akkadian Empire tried to solve that problem. It then turns to a still-debated question: why, roughly a century and a half later, did the empire collapse?
📚 STANDARDIZING AN EMPIRE

Sargon and his successors tried a truly new plan for ruling. The best-known of these successors was his grandson, Naram-Sin. Instead of leaving each conquered city fully to its own local rulers and customs, Sargon's dynasty put Akkadian-picked governors over conquered cities. They pushed the Akkadian language, a language apart from Sumerian, alongside Sumerian in state business, and worked to make weights, measures, and how things were run the same across the empire's many cities.

Naram-Sin went further than any Akkadian king before him. He took the title "King of the Four Quarters," meaning king of the whole known world. In some old tales, he even claimed to be a god himself during his own life. Kings before Naram-Sin mostly served the gods. Naram-Sin, in this telling, tried to stand next to them instead.
📚 THE CURSE OF AKKAD'S EXPLANATION

And then, within a few generations, the Akkadian Empire fell apart. A Sumerian poem called the **Curse of Akkad** gives a sharp reason why. In the poem's telling, Naram-Sin defied the will of the great god Enlil and tore down Enlil's own temple, the Ekur at Nippur. In reply, Enlil cursed the city of Akkad itself, brought famine down on the land, and called on a fierce people from the mountains, the Gutians, to overrun it. In this telling, hubrisHYOO-brisa king or hero's dangerous, excessive pride, especially pride that leads someone to defy the gods or ignore real limits., a king's excess pride, calls down the wrath of the gods.

section: WEIGHING AN ANCIENT EXPLANATION AGAINST A MODERN ONE
text: 📚 WEIGHING AN ANCIENT EXPLANATION AGAINST A MODERN ONE

section: WEIGHING AN ANCIENT EXPLANATION AGAINST A MODERN ONE
text: This old reason is worth taking with real weight, on its own terms, rather than pushing it aside. Modern historians work from clues the ancient poem's author never had. Studies of old soil and pollen layers show a long, hard drought hit the region around the time of Akkad's fall, which would have strained the canal-fed farming Sumer relied on. The poem itself also names Gutian raids from the Zagros Mountains, which historians think were most likely real events too, even though the poem frames them as payback sent by the gods.

section: WEIGHING AN ANCIENT EXPLANATION AGAINST A MODERN ONE
text: Do not ask "which single cause is the whole answer?" A drought does not, by itself, force a king to defy the priests of Enlil. A moral flaw does not, by itself, dry up a river. Both threads were very likely at work together. Notice, too, that Akkad's fall does not fit a story of steady progress. Great empires can decline and fall apart; they do not simply grow stronger forever, and the reasons why are rarely simple. The Bronze Age Collapse will ask this same question again, at a much larger scale.
👥 PEOPLES · THE GUTIANS

Mesopotamian texts describe the Gutians as mountain people from the Zagros range, living outside the city-based world of Sumer and Akkad. Because nearly every surviving description of the Gutians was written by their enemies, historians treat these descriptions cautiously, as evidence of how Mesopotamians viewed outsiders as much as evidence of the Gutians themselves.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · NARAM-SIN
Photo: Rama, CC BY-SA 2.0 France, via Wikimedia Commons.

**Naram-Sin** ruled the Akkadian Empire as Sargon's grandson, around 2254 to 2218 BC. He expanded the empire further than Sargon had, took the title "King of the Four Quarters," and, according to some ancient traditions, claimed divine status during his own lifetime. His famous victory stele shows him trampling defeated enemies while wearing the horned crown normally reserved for gods.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

The first empire in recorded history rose on a string of small, uncertain events and fell for reasons that are still debated today. Hold both halves of that story together: Sargon's rise and Akkad's fall are the same lesson, that history does not march toward one guaranteed outcome, told twice.

section: What is a grand building project actually for?
text: Nineveh fell to a combined Babylonian-Median army in 612 BC, leaving Babylon free to build its own empire. This lesson meets Nebuchadnezzar II, whose Ishtar Gate, ziggurat, and glazed-brick walls turned Babylon into one of the most famous cities of the ancient world, and asks what a project like that is actually for: not shelter or storage, but a political statement in stone and color.
