section: PART 1 WHO CAME, AND ON WHAT TERMS
PART 1 WHO CAME, AND ON WHAT TERMS
text: The first three hundred families to receive land under Austin's grant, remembered as the Old Three Hundred, came overwhelmingly from Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana, the part of the United States sometimes called the Old Southwest. In exchange for a **league** of grazing land and a **labor** of farmland, nearly free, colonists swore an oath of loyalty and agreed to practice Catholicism, though enforcement of the religious requirement was often loose in practice.
💡 HELPFUL TO KNOW

Austin was not the only empresario working this system. Erasmo Seguín, a Tejano ally who had helped negotiate the original grant, and fellow empresarios Martín De León and Green DeWitt were bringing in colonists of their own around the same years. Austin's colony was the largest and best documented, not the only one.

section: PART 1 A REPORT, THEN A LAW
text: 📚 PART 1 · A REPORT, THEN A LAW

section: PART 1 A REPORT, THEN A LAW
text: In 1828, the Mexican official Manuel de Mier y Terán inspected Texas and reported back to Mexico City. What he found alarmed officials there: Anglo settlement was outpacing Mexican population and control across the province. The Law of April 6, 1830, was Mexico City's direct response. It halted further immigration from the United States and stepped up customs enforcement along the coast.
⚠️ WATCH OUT

Notice the cause and effect here. Mier y Terán's report does not cause a crisis by itself; it is Mexico City's policy response to that report, the Law of April 6, that actually lands on the colonists and starts the confrontation.

section: PART 2 ANAHUAC, TURTLE BAYOU, AND THE CONVENTIONS
text: 📚 PART 2 · ANAHUAC, TURTLE BAYOU, AND THE CONVENTIONS

section: PART 2 ANAHUAC, TURTLE BAYOU, AND THE CONVENTIONS
text: Enforcement of the new customs rules at the garrison town of Anahuac provoked open resistance in 1832. The colonists involved issued the Turtle Bayou Resolutions, which declared loyalty not to Mexico's centralist government but to the federalists and to General Santa Anna, who was then leading a movement against the same centralizing policies. Notice what this loyalty statement is not: it is not yet a declaration of independence from Mexico.

PART 2 ANAHUAC, TURTLE BAYOU, AND THE CONVENTIONS
text: The Conventions of 1832 and 1833 turned these grievances into formal petitions. Read carefully what colonists actually asked for at these conventions: statehood for Texas within Mexico, repeal of the Law of April 6, relief from customs tariffs, and trial by jury, the same grievance that had been building. None of it asked for separation from Mexico.

Every colonist petition still asks for a place inside Mexico, not outside it. Hold that carefully.

section: PART 1 WHY THIS HAD NEVER WORKED BEFORE
text: Cavalry had tried to solve the mounted-firearms problem before. The caracole, riders firing a single shot then wheeling away to reload, was tried for roughly a century and eventually abandoned. Dragoons sometimes dismounted just to get one good shot off. In every case, giving up the mounted charge to fire a single shot was never worth the tradeoff against a continuously-reloading mounted opponent. section: PART 2 A CREEK BED, AND A REVERSAL IN POLICY

section: PART 2 A CREEK BED, AND A REVERSAL IN POLICY
text: In June 1844, Ranger captain Jack Hays led roughly fifteen men against a far larger Comanche force at Walker's Creek, and fought the entire engagement from the saddle using Paterson revolvers. It worked. Samuel Walker later worked directly with Colt to design an improved model, the Walker Colt, in 1847; the U.S. Army ordered a thousand of them, and Colt's company, bankrupt only five years earlier, began its rise from a Texas creek bed.
💡 HELPFUL TO KNOW

Tonkawa scouts worked closely with the Rangers throughout this period, while the Waco were present at the Tehuacana Creek councils when Houston returned to office and reversed Lamar's policy. Indian groups on this frontier had varied, sometimes opposing relationships with Texans; there was no single, uniform position.

A federal constitution promises Texas real power. A merger with a bigger neighbor takes much of it back.

The Mexican federal Constitution of 1824 is the legal foundation of Texan home rule. But Texas was not made its own state. It was merged with its larger neighbor as "Coahuila y Tejas," and colonists felt the effects of that merger almost immediately.

💡 GLOSSARY OF SUBJECT VOCABULARY
One word is worth reviewing before you read.
**federalism** (FED-er-uh-liz-um) — a system of government in which power is divided between a national government and individual states, with states holding real authority of their own.

text: 📚 PART 1 · ONE EMPRESARIO BREAKS THE PATTERN

section: PART 1 ONE EMPRESARIO BREAKS THE PATTERN
text: Keeping the Mexican form and working inside it was not the only response available. In 1826, empresario Haden Edwards had his own grant revoked by Mexican authorities over a land dispute. Edwards and a small band of followers responded by declaring their own short-lived "Republic of Fredonia" in East Texas. It collapsed within months, and notably, Austin's own colonial militia helped Mexican forces put it down. Austin's colonists, still working the system rather than breaking from it, saw Fredonia as a reckless exception, not a model to follow.
⚠️ WATCH OUT

Hold onto the irony here. Austin helps suppress a rebellion against Mexican authority in 1827. Six years later, he will be arrested for disloyalty to that same authority. Watch how his relationship with Mexico City actually changes between these two moments.

The bigger political story that same decade was the federal **federalism** written into Mexico's Constitution of 1824, drawn partly from the United States' own constitutional model and partly from Spain's earlier Constitution of 1812. On paper, this gave Texas a real claim to self-governing power as part of a Mexican state.
📚 PART 2 · OUTVOTED FROM THE START

Texas was not given its own statehood. It was attached to its larger neighbor as the single state of "Coahuila y Tejas," with its capital at Saltillo, hundreds of miles from most Texas settlements. Texas colonists were consistently outvoted by Coahuila's larger population, and the province's own courts sat a long ride away. Petitions asking for separate statehood begin almost immediately after the merger, and they never really stop for the rest of the decade.

One more federal decision from this period touched the colony directly. In 1829, Mexico's government issued a decree abolishing slavery nationwide. In practice, Texas received a special exemption, and colonists who still wanted enslaved labor increasingly relied on a legal workaround: binding enslaved people under long-term "indentured servant" contracts that Mexican authorities mostly tolerated rather than enforced against.
💡 HELPFUL TO KNOW
This is the same pattern showing up again: a Mexican law stays on the books, and colonists build a practical workaround that keeps the law's form while changing what actually happens underneath it.
💪 CARRY THIS FORWARD
Federalism promised Texas real power; the Coahuila y Tejas merger delivered a much thinner version of it in practice.
